extract:
The Killers formed in Las Vegas, Nevada in 2001, emerging from a desert city not previously known as an incubator for indie or alternative rock. Frontman Brandon Flowers, a Utah-raised synth-pop devotee, met guitarist Dave Keuning after responding to a classified ad Keuning had placed in a local weekly. The lineup solidified with bassist Mark Stoermer and drummer Ronnie Vannucci Jr., and the band began playing small Vegas clubs like the Junkyard while soaking up the transatlantic post-punk revival then sweeping through New York and London. Their formative touchstones were unmistakable: the anthemic sweep of U2, the arch romanticism of Morrissey and the Smiths, the synth textures of Duran Duran and New Order, and the leather-jacket cool of contemporaries like Interpol and the Strokes.

After being turned down by American labels, the band signed to the London indie Lizard King, with Island handling the U.S. release, and issued their debut Hot Fuss in 2004. Built around the singles Mr. Brightside, Somebody Told Me, All These Things That I've Done, and Smile Like You Mean It, the record fused new wave keyboards with muscular guitar hooks and Flowers's theatrical delivery, becoming one of the defining alternative albums of the decade. Mr. Brightside in particular achieved a near-mythic afterlife, charting in the UK for a record-shattering number of consecutive weeks and becoming a karaoke and stadium staple long after its release.

For 2006's Sam's Town, produced by Flood and Alan Moulder, the band pivoted sharply toward heartland Americana, invoking Bruce Springsteen and Tom Petty in tracks like When You Were Young and the title cut. The pivot puzzled some critics at the time but has aged into one of their most beloved statements, with Read My Mind emerging as a fan favorite. Day & Age (2008), produced by Stuart Price, swung back to synths and disco pulse with Human and Spaceman, while 2012's Battle Born aimed for widescreen rock ambition. Along the way Flowers pursued a solo career with Flamingo and The Desired Effect, and the band contributed to holiday charity singles and various one-off collaborations, including work with New Order's Bernard Sumner and Pet Shop Boys touchstones that reinforced their British new-wave lineage.

Later albums Wonderful Wonderful (2017), Imploding the Mirage (2020), and Pressure Machine (2021) saw the group working with producers like Jacknife Lee and Shawn Everett, with Imploding the Mirage in particular winning strong reviews for its widescreen, Fleetwood Mac–inflected rock. Pressure Machine, written during the pandemic, was a quieter, narrative-driven record rooted in Flowers's memories of small-town Nephi, Utah, and featured a guest turn from Phoebe Bridgers. Keuning and Stoermer stepped back from touring during this period, though they remained connected to the band.

Critically, The Killers occupy a rare position: a stadium-filling rock act whose signature song keeps gaining cultural velocity nearly two decades after release, and whose catalog spans glossy synth-pop, Americana, and gospel-tinged arena rock. They continue to tour globally, headlining festivals like Glastonbury, and stand as the most commercially successful rock band Las Vegas has ever produced, a legacy sealed by Hot Fuss's enduring ubiquity.
title: The Killers
